children: The antecedent noun to the pronoun “they” could also be more “souls,” or it could be “stars.” “Twilight phantoms” above already seems to fall back on “stars,” but the mention of “structure, haunches, necks, and skulls points to the mare and her fillyfoal. That the pronoun "she” wants to point back to “soul,” especially inasmuch as the soul is used repeatedly in
Ulysses
Portrait of the Artist

, and in classical literature generally using the feminine gender, makes it hard to argue that we are not talking about a soul (of either gender) and its mother (or father if we’re using “feminine” as  gender-neutral in reference to souls).
The section suggesting the style of De Quincy notwithstanding , to this point it seems to bear a strong, but satirical, correlation to Wordsworth’s
Ode: Imitations of Immortality

, notably, its fifth stanza, especially if we’re talking about souls here. To begin with, the stanza begins with the words “Our birth.” The birth process, Mrs. Purefoy giving birth as the chapter’s setting, the theme of the disinclination of Irish youth in contributing to the volume of Irish births, all leave a strong link. Wordsworth’s “Soul that rises with us,” he describes as, “our life’s Star points to a "scattered … perennial dew of stars here”. Forms of the word “cloud” are used three times in Joyce’s passage. Wordsworth claims that it is “trailing clouds of glory [that we do] come/From God, who is our home.” The Ode’s serene soul “cometh from afar,"lying on its cloud, forgetting and asleep. Joyce’s "souls” come on a misty highway “muttering thunder of rebellion, the ghosts of beasts.” It must be noted that De Quincy was very closely associated with Wordsworth, lived near him in the Lake District, and wrote a series of reminiscences of the great poet.
Agendath Nataim is a very important symbol in
Ulysses

; the reference appears thirteen separate times in the novel as a promised land, despite the disparagement it appears to receive in this instance – another reason I believe the insolence of the souls in the passage is also meant as irony. The  ad  he had seen earlier in the day calling on European Jews like himself to become part of the cultivation of Palestine, a restoration of Zion, and the poorly drafted, disjointed, contradiction-laden notice brings to Bloom’s mind the fecklessness of the Celtic revivalist movement in resolving the persistent problems of identity for Ireland. It is of Ireland and not Palestine of which Joyce is speaking here as “a waste land, a home of screechowls and the sandblind upupa,” (a weak-sighted bird that lines its nest with human excrement).

children: In the book of Judges in the Bible, Gideon is called upon to lead a relatively small force of Israelites against a massive army of Middianites. Gideon wanted to make sure God was with him, so he proposed a test; “Behold, I will put a fleece of wool in the floor; and if the dew be on the fleece only, and it be dry upon the earth beside, this shall I know that thou wilt save Israel by my hand, as thou has said.” As indicated here, on the morrow the fleece was not just wet, it was drenched, and so Gideon was able to successfully lead a group that was whittled down to 300 men against the opposing army of 130,000, suggesting God’s abundant favor.

This entire passage honors Theodore Purefoy, and extols his virtues, having sired the newly born infant. Of course, the father’s role here is minimal, given without any thought of creating a new person. But, at least he is married, and he is not doing anything to prevent conception as he engages with his wife. This is high satire, in that it is the wife who faces the ordeal of  nine months of pregnancy and the painful process of labor and delivery. As we have seen before, the references in the chapter, as throughout
Ulysses

, deal with the process of literary creation. Joyce implies, once again, that fatherhood is not as true a trope for that process as is motherhood, and that the course of creating superior literary art takes time and great and often painful effort.
